paper_title: HiP3R: Hierarchical Pose Graphs for Long-Horizon 3D Reconstruction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Feed-forward models accurately estimate camera motion and 3D geometry from short video windows. However, computational and memory costs prevent direct inference on sequences containing thousands of frames. Long videos must therefore be processed as overlapping chunks. This division produces independent local reconstructions with inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate estimates of shared cameras. Achieving global consistency requires propagating constraints from adjacent overlaps and distant revisits across the sequence. This requirement naturally motivates pose graph optimization. However, the choice of graph level creates a trade-off. Chunk-level graphs efficiently resolve scale drift and close large loops. Yet, their rigid transformations cannot correct internal errors or conflicting frame predictions. Conversely, frame-level optimization offers local flexibility, but scaling it globally is computationally expensive and can break metric scale. HiP3R resolves this trade-off using a hierarchical pose graph. HiP3R first optimizes a robust chunk-level $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ graph to establish the global layout and scale. It then holds this layout fixed and estimates one shared $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ camera per frame, turning overlapping window predictions into a single trajectory. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of HiP3R in improving camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction. Our method applies to both chunk-based and streaming backends without additional training or fine-tuning. The codes are available at https://kkakkkka.github.io/HiP3R.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recovering globally consistent 3D geometry and camera trajectories from video is fundamental to computer vision. This capability supports autonomous navigation, robotic mapping, and spatial artificial intelligence. Recent 3D foundation models (Wang et al., 2024; 2025a; 2026b) have significantly advanced visual geometry. By jointly predicting camera poses and dense pointmaps in single forward pass, they bypass classical handcrafted matching. These models achieve high accuracy on short video clips without per-scene calibration or optimization. However, the quadratic complexity of visual attention limits them to short temporal windows. Directly scaling transformers to extended multi-kilometer sequences remains too expensive. To process long videos, modern systems adopt divide-and-conquer strategy (Deng et al., 2025). Long sequences are divided into overlapping video chunks, which are processed independently and stitched together. While chunking bounds GPU memory, sequential alignment introduces severe computational and numerical bottlenecks. Dense overlapping points share high spatial redundancy, making all-pixel alignment computationally expensive. Furthermore, pairwise alignment errors compound along the sequential chain, causing severe scale and orientation drift. Loop closures are essential to eliminate cumulative drift and enforce global topological consistency. However, when the chains are not yet aligned, applying multiple long-range loop constraints at once can make the non-convex optimization unstable. The solver may diverge or converge to poor local minima. As shown in Figure 1, even after global chunk placement is resolved, conflict remains at the frame level. Existing alignment methods (Deng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Xiong et al., 2026) optimize similarity transformations per chunk. Arbitrarily selecting one prediction discards multi-view evidence and causes velocity jumps across chunk boundaries. Conversely, full bundle adjustment is too expensive, while relative motion alone drifts from the recovered global layout. To overcome these challenges, we introduce HIP3R, Hierarchical Pose-graph optimization method for long-horizon 3D Reconstruction. HIP3R decomposes reconstruction into coarse chunk layout recovery and fine frame trajectory refinement. The coarse stage optimizes chunk-level Sim(3) pose graph over adjacent overlaps and distant loop closures. This stage establishes globally consistent layout and eliminates accumulated scale drift. Holding this coarse layout fixed, the fine stage optimizes frame-level shared-camera SE(3) pose graph, representing each physical frame with single camera variable to resolve cross-window pose inconsistency. Placement priors keep that camera on the recovered layout, while within-chunk motion factors resolve conflicting predictions from overlapping windows. We evaluate HIP3R across seven public benchmarks spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments. Under matched backends and windows, HIP3R improves long-horizon trajectory accuracy over loop-enabled VGGT-Long. Controlled ablations show that bounded point sampling reduces graph construction and optimization time with little change in accuracy. Additional evaluations show that the method also works with streaming backends such as LingBot-MAP. We summarize our main contributions as follows: We show that chunk-level similarity alignment alone cannot ensure cross-window camera-pose consistency, as overlapping windows may yield conflicting estimates for the same frame. We develop hierarchical pose graph that first recovers globally consistent chunk layout and scale, then estimates one shared SE(3) camera pose for each frame. We introduce progressive loop closure and bounded point sampling to achieve stable and scalable optimization on long sequences without retraining.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Feed-forward 3D vision models. Feed-forward 3D models have emerged as an alternative to classical Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Subsequent models explore permutation invariance (Wang et al., 2025c), sparse attention (Wang et al., 2026a), and learned scene actions (Wang & Agapito, 2026). sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate trajectory accuracy across seven public benchmarks comprising 61 diverse sequences. The benchmark spans indoor room-scale environments, including 7-Scenes (Shotton et al., 2013) and Neural RGB-D (Azinovic et al., 2022). It also includes high-precision multi-scale scenes from ETH3D (Schops et al., 2017) and Tanks and Temples (Knapitsch et al., 2017). Finally, it includes extended outdoor driving and campus traversals from Oxford Spires (Tao et al., 2025), KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012), and VBR (Brizi et al., 2024). Dense surface geometry is evaluated on ETH3D, Neural RGB-D, and 7-Scenes, which provide dense 3D ground truth. Appendix details dataset compositions and sequence splits. Baselines in Table 1 use released checkpoints and recommended window policies on identical sequences. VGGT-Long and VGGT-Align are evaluated from public implementations, while VGGT-Motion (Xiong et al., 2026) is not publicly available. We evaluate trajectory accuracy using ATE, RPErot, and RPEtrans (lower is better). ATE is translation RMSE after per-sequence Sim(3) alignment that corrects rotation, translation, and scale. Relative errors use all consecutive frame pairs (=1 frame). Rotation RPE is in degrees, and translation RPE applies the same Sim(3) correction. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: HIP3R turns overlapping local predictions into globally consistent reconstruction of long video sequences through hierarchical pose graph. The method first recovers global layout and scale through chunk-level Sim(3) graph, then refines shared-camera SE(3) graph with the chunk transforms held fixed. This separation allows distant loop closures to correct accumulated drift while reconciling conflicting predictions of the same camera across windows. Evaluations on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show improvements in overall trajectory accuracy and surface reconstruction with both VGGT-Omega and LingBot-MAP. Extending this hierarchy to online updates and improving its robustness to unreliable loop closures are promising directions for future work.

sections.title: E DATASETS AND SPLITS
sections.content: We evaluate HIP3R across seven public benchmarks spanning 61 diverse sequences. Table 11 lists dataset compositions, sensor domains, and evaluation properties. Indoor room-scale and multi-scale sequences. These three datasets evaluate performance across local and multi-scale settings with varying sequence lengths and scene complexity. With the default VGGT-Omega chunk size of 60 frames and overlap size of 30 frames, 10 of the 11 ETH3D still sequences fit within single chunk. For these sequences, the layout and shared-camera graphs remain inactive, and the Native, Layout Only, and Full trajectories coincide. Neural RGB-D spans 211 chunks per sequence, while 7-Scenes spans 36. 7-Scenes (Shotton et al., 2013) consists of seven Kinect-captured rooms: Chess, Fire, Heads, Office, Pumpkin, Kitchen, and Stairs. ETH3D (Schops et al., 2017) includes high-resolution indoor and outdoor still sequences with laser-scanner ground truth, covering offices, reliefs, facades, playgrounds, and gardens. Neural RGB-D (Azinovic et al., 2022) contains nine room-scale indoor scenes with structured-light depth, including kitchens, staircases, and apartments. Outdoor structures and buildings. Tanks and Temples (Knapitsch et al., 2017) evaluates Barn, Caterpillar, Courthouse, Ignatius, Meeting Room, and Truck. Extended traversals and driving loops. Oxford Spires (Tao et al., 2025) provides nine campus sequences with LiDAR-inertial ground truth, subsampled to 320 frames. The sequences mix outdoor courtyards, interiors, and staircases, with revisits after long temporal gaps. KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) uses odometry sequence 00 only (T =4541), standard benchmark for long driving loops. VBR (Brizi et al., 2024) contains seven long urban sequences through Rome, 8,81518,846 frames per sequence (dataset-mean =12,383). Additional keyframe and layout-solver experiments use the downtown1, downtown2, and downtown5 sequences from Droid-W (Li et al., 2026a). Aggregation. Trajectory benchmark metrics are averaged within each dataset and then equally across the seven datasets. Dense geometry metrics use an equal-weight average over the 38 evaluated sequences, as detailed in Appendix H.

sections.title: I CHUNK AND OVERLAP EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Table 18 compares selected chunk and overlap sizes against fixed defaults in an exploratory sweep. The default chunk size and overlap size are 60 and 30 frames for VGGT-Omega, and 120 and 32 frames for LingBot-MAP. Each window configuration produces its own chunk predictions and optimized coarse layout, which is then held fixed during camera processing. The coarse solve follows Appendix D, with limit of 5000 function evaluations. Both window configurations use dense fine optimization for 2000 and overlap consensus for longer sequences. Overlap consensus averages rotations and translations at stride-10 frames, retains the final frame, and interpolates pose corrections to the remaining frames. For long sequences, this replaces the stride-5 keyframe optimization used in the main benchmark. On KITTI, LingBot-MAP achieves 3.508 with overlap consensus, compared with 6.063 for Full in Table 13. Selected versus default macro-averaged ATE across the seven datasets is 4.403 versus 4.908 for VGGT-Omega, and 3.822 versus 3.825 for LingBot-MAP. ABLATION ON THE COARSE-ONLY LAYOUT Table 19 compares camera accuracy after the coarse layout stage alone against the Full pipeline on three long sequences. Shared-camera refinement lowers RPErot and RPEtrans on all three sequences while leaving ATE close to the coarse-stage result.

All evaluated configurations share identical model predictions, candidate revisit pairs, and initialization. Camera refinement and point corrections are disabled to isolate layout optimization. The full coarse solve allows at most 5000 function evaluations. The five configurations evaluate baseline pairwise alignment, bounded point sampling, residual-fit weighting, progressive loop scheduling, and the complete optimization solver. The final step combines adaptive continuation, Huber loss, and bounded restarts. Appendix specifies the continuation and restart rules and their evaluation budgets. We test solver robustness against noisy loop measurements by perturbing loop closures. Specifically, synthetic noise is injected into 25% of detected loop edges using fixed random seed. For each selected edge, we apply 10 rotation error. We also inject 25% translation offset and 0.10 log-scale distortion. The evaluation confirms efficiency gains from bounded sampling, alongside accuracy and runtime gains from the complete solver. The complete configuration reduces clean mean ATE by 19.77% relative to the baseline. This improvement concentrates in VBR, where mean error falls from 28.6017 to 22.4461 m. Peak host memory remains comparable across configurations.

sections.title: L PLACEMENT AND MOTION ABLATION SETTINGS
sections.content: The four controls in Table 5 evaluate different strategies for resolving multiple camera predictions under identical optimized coarse layouts. Layout Only selects the first available coarse-placed pose for each frame in chunk order. Single selects the occurrence that maximizes the minimum distance, in frames, to either boundary of its chunk. Ties are broken by the smaller chunk index. Both Layout Only and Single directly output the selected coarse-placed poses without frame-level optimization. Unary computes robust pose average over all coarse-placed occurrences of each frame using deterministic Huber IRLS, without relative-motion factors. Motion optimizes withinchunk relative-motion factors without placement priors. It fixes the first camera to its coarse placement and uses λf = 1 and λp = 0. This control allows up to 5000 function evaluations with ftol = xtol = gtol = 108. Shared jointly optimizes placement priors and relative-motion constraints as formulated in Eq. (6), and corresponds to Full in the main benchmark. All configurations use the same evaluation protocol, and results are macro-averaged across all seven datasets.
